chapters.title: Chapter 3: Reading Trade War Signals as an Investor

lessons.title: Building a Trade War Watchlist: Indicators Every Indian Investor Should Track

children.text: You have covered the tools countries use, how those tools transmit into Indian markets, and how to hedge and rotate around them. This closing lesson assembles all of it into one watchlist you can actually maintain, five tiers, checked at different frequencies, that together turn "trade war hits markets" from a reaction into a process.
Each tier below maps back to something you have already learned. None of it needs to be checked constantly; the table tells you the actual cadence each tier deserves.

cells: 1. Policy & Sources
New tariff or exemption notifications affecting sectors you hold
Weekly, or immediately on a breaking headline
USTR, DGFT, Federal Register
2. Macro Market Signals
DXY, USD/INR spot and forward premium, Brent crude, gold
Daily glance, deeper look only on unusual moves
Financial data feeds, RBI publications
3. Capital Flow Signals
India VIX, daily FII/DII net flow data
Daily
NSE website, broker platforms
4. Sector & Company Signals
Direct-exposure sectors (textiles, gems & jewellery, seafood, metals, autos), concall commentary on your holdings
Ongoing for existing holdings, deep dive each results season
screener.in, company investor relations pages, exchange filings
5. Domestic Overlay Check
Concurrent budget, RBI policy, or election-cycle catalysts that could be misread as trade-war-driven
Whenever a big market move needs explaining
Budget documents, RBI monetary policy statements, financial press

children.text: A Full Scenario: Putting It All Together

body.title: Read the Whole Morning
body.scenario: It's a Tuesday morning. Overnight, the USTR website posted a notice proposing an additional 15% tariff on auto components from India, with a 30-day comment period before it takes effect. DXY is up 0.8%, Brent crude is down 2%, and India VIX has risen 9%. Yesterday's provisional exchange data showed FIIs as net sellers for the fourth straight session. Separately, this is also Union Budget week, and early reports suggest a possible change to capital gains tax treatment for equity investors.
body.prompt: Using all five tiers of the watchlist, walk through how you would read this morning, and what, if anything, you would actually do.
body.modelAnswer: Tier 1: a 30-day comment period means this is a proposal, not yet a binding cost, and an exemption request window is still open, so it is a real signal to track for any auto component holdings, not a reason to sell immediately. Tier 2: DXY up and crude down is a fairly typical risk-off combination for a tariff scare, with the falling oil price acting as a partial offset to the rupee pressure. Tier 3: four straight sessions of FII selling plus a 9% VIX jump shows the capital flow channel is active, worth monitoring closely. Tier 4: this is a direct hit for auto component holdings specifically, review that position's actual US revenue exposure and check whether management already addressed tariff risk in the last concall, other unrelated sector holdings need no action. Tier 5, and this is the critical step: Union Budget week with a capital gains tax rumor is a major concurrent domestic catalyst that could easily be driving a meaningful share of the FII selling and VIX spike on its own, independent of the USTR notice. Before treating this as purely a trade war morning, check how much of the move persists after the budget details are actually announced, that is the test that separates a real trade-war signal from a budget-week coincidence wearing a trade war headline.

body.title: The Single Most Useful Habit
body.question: Which of the following is the most reliable way to confirm a market move is genuinely trade-war-driven rather than a domestic-specific story wearing the same headline?
options: Check whether the Nifty fell more than 1% that day
Check whether other emerging markets are moving in the same direction, for the same reason, at the same time
Check what financial news anchors are saying about it
Check whether the specific stocks you own fell
body.explanation: A genuinely global trade war shock rarely hits India in isolation. If other emerging markets are not moving for the same reason at the same time, there is a good chance a domestic-specific catalyst, like August 2019's FPI surcharge, is doing some or all of the work instead.

body.text: A watchlist is not a trading signal generator. Checking these five tiers regularly builds pattern recognition; on most days, nothing on this list will actually warrant a portfolio change. The discipline this course is really teaching is not reacting to noise, not reacting fast.

A trade war is not one event you either dodge or get hit by. It is a slow, multi-stage process: tariffs, sanctions, and currency policy at the source; the rupee, commodities, and capital flows in transmission; and specific sectors and companies at the point of impact. Read each stage, and a trade war stops being noise you react to and becomes a pattern you can actually trade around.

points: Trade wars run on three tools, tariffs, sanctions, and currency policy, and are defined by a retaliation cycle, not any single policy move (Chapter 1).
They transmit into Indian markets through currency, commodities, and capital flows, and land unevenly across sectors: direct losers, carve-outs, indirect losers, and quiet winners (Chapter 2).

The single most useful habit in this entire course is separating genuinely global, trade-war-driven moves from domestic-specific catalysts wearing the same headline, the way August 2019's FPI surcharge got blended into a global trade war narrative.

A five-tier watchlist, policy sources, macro market signals, capital flows, sector and company signals, and a domestic overlay check, turns that reading skill into a repeatable weekly and daily routine (Chapter 3).
Most days, the correct response to a trade war headline is still no action at all. The watchlist exists to tell you when that changes.
